newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turkish cordon in N. Iraq unacceptable - Baghdad.
newsitem.headline: Turkish cordon in N. Iraq unacceptable - Baghdad.

text.p: Baghdad on Friday attacked Turkey's plans to create a security buffer zone in Iraq's northern Kurdish region, and called on its Arab neighbours to support it against the United States.

"We have heard during the past two days that Turkey intends to create a so-called security zone," senior undersecretary of the foreign ministry Saad al-Faisel said in an interview with state-run television.
"We formally and categorically reject it. We shall not accept this because it constitutes a violation of Iraq's sovereignty. It is unacceptable and we have informed the Turks of this," he said.
Faisel did not say what measures Iraq might take to prevent Turkey from taking such a step. He said it was in Ankara's interest to coordinate with Baghdad to solve problems in its north.

He urged Turkey to end the presence of Western NATO troops on its territory providing protection for Iraqi Kurds. "Once these troops leave...the Kurds would then desire to forge agreement with the (Iraqi) central government," Faisel said.
Earlier, Iraq summoned the Turkish acting charge d'affaires in Baghdad to complain about Ankara's military build-up along the border with Kurdish-held northern Iraq.
Turkey is planning to create a security zone in northern Iraq up to 10 km (six miles) deep and Washington said on Wednesday it would not object if Ankara went ahead with the scheme.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Friday the cordon would deter infiltration from Iraq by guerrillas of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), fighting for self-rule in Turkey's Kurdish southeast.
In the interview, Faisel also called on member countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to back it against "the evil forces" of the United States.

"There will be a GCC meeting on Saturday. And from here I urge the brethren in the Arab Gulf to take in their meeting a stand in support of Iraq against the evil and infidel forces of America," he said.

Pointing out that U.S. and allied warplanes had used Saudi and Kuwaiti bases in their patrols of the southern Iraq no-fly zone, he said he hoped Arab Gulf countries realised "the seriousness of this action which America undertakes from their territory".
The United States fired a total of 44 cruise missiles on Tuesday and Wednesday at air defence targets in southern Iraq to minimise Iraqi resistance to allied patrols over an expanded no-fly zone.
Baghdad has made repeated overtures particularly to Kuwait -- which it invaded in 1990 -- and Saudi Arabia since the 1991 Gulf War, but to no avail.
Faisel said it was time to forget the past and it would be "in nobody's interest to open past wounds".
He said he noted positive stands over the latest U.S. missile strikes against Iraq from the GCC member states United Arab Emirates (UAE), Qatar, Oman and Bahrain, apart from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.
